Every week, we break down topics like
this one, real and practical health
information made simple, especially for
people in their 60s, 70s, and beyond.
Subscribing helps more people find these
videos, and it helps us keep making
them. Now, let's get into it.
Let's start with the basics, in plain
language, because many people have never
had these two numbers explained
properly.
Your blood pressure is the force of your
blood pushing against the walls of your
arteries as your heart pumps it around
your body.
Think of a garden hose. If the water is
turned on gently, the pressure inside
the hose is low. If the tap is opened
fully, or if the hose becomes narrow and
stiff, the pressure inside rises. The
top number is called the systolic
pressure. This is the pressure in your
arteries at the moment your heart
squeezes and pushes blood out.
The bottom number is called the
diastolic pressure. This is the pressure
in your arteries when your heart relaxes
between beats and refills with blood.
So, when someone says your blood
pressure is 130 over 80, it means the
pressure was 130 when your heart was
squeezing and 80 when your heart was
resting between beats.
Now, here is the first important point.
Both numbers matter, but as we get
older, the top number, the systolic
pressure, becomes the one that doctors
watch most closely.
Let me explain why.
When we are younger, our arteries are
soft and flexible, like a new rubber
hose.
When the heart pushes blood into them,
they stretch a little and then spring
back, which keeps the pressure smooth
and steady.
But, over the years, our arteries
naturally become stiffer.
This happens to almost everyone, even
healthy people who have never smoked and
have always eaten well.
The walls lose some of their elasticity,
a little like an old garden hose that
has been left out in the sun for many
summers.
When the arteries are stiffer, they
cannot absorb the push of each heartbeat
as well. So, the top number tends to
rise with age, while the bottom number
often stays the same or even drifts
slightly lower.
This pattern is so common in older
adults that it even has a name.
It is called isolated systolic
hypertension, where the top number is
high, but the bottom number is normal or
low.
So, if you are over 65 and your reading
looks like 150 over 70, you are not
unusual. This is one of the most common
patterns I see, and it is also one of
the patterns that deserves attention,
because a high top number is strongly
linked with the risk of stroke and heart
problems.
Now, you may be asking, "Dr. Malik, if
arteries stiffen with age, shouldn't the
ideal number simply go up as we get
older?"
That is exactly the question many people
ask, and it is where the confusion
begins,
because the answer, honestly, is no, Not
automatically.
Stiffer arteries are a reason why the
number tends to rise.
They are not a reason to accept a high
number as a normal part of getting
older.
A high number is still a risk, even if
it is common.
So, what do the major guidelines
actually say?
I want to be careful here because
different medical organizations around
the world have slightly different
recommendations, and they have changed
over the years. So, I will explain the
general picture rather than quote one
single rule.
For many years, a commonly used target
for older adults was to keep the top
number below 150.
Then, a large study in the United
States, followed by updated guidelines,
led many experts to recommend a lower
target for most adults, including many
older adults, often below 130 over 80.
Some studies even suggested that aiming
for an even lower top number, around
120, reduced the risk of heart attacks,
strokes, and heart failure in certain
groups of older adults.
At the same time, other respected
guidelines, including some in Europe,
suggest that for people over 65, a top
number somewhere in the range of 130 to
139 is a reasonable target if it is well
tolerated, and that older adults should
not be pushed too low.
So, even among experts, you will see
slightly different advice.
And that is not because they are
confused, it is because the right target
depends on the person.
The studies that showed benefit from
lower targets also showed something
else. Pushing the pressure lower led to
more side effects in some people, such
as dizziness, fainting, kidney strain,
and changes in salt and potassium levels
in the blood.
This is why I tell my patients that the
ideal blood pressure after 65 is not a
single number. It is a range that your
doctor chooses for you, based on your
overall health, your medications, your
risk of falling, and how you feel at
different readings.
Let me explain what I mean by how you
feel at different readings, because this
is something many people have never been
told. I once cared for a gentleman in
his early 70s. He was careful,
disciplined, and proud of how well he
followed his doctor's advice. His blood
pressure readings at home were often
around 108 over 62.
He told me proudly that it was better
than when he was a young man. But as we
talked, he mentioned that every morning
when he got out of bed and stood up too
quickly, the room would spin for a few
seconds. He had nearly fallen twice.
He had also been feeling unusually tired
in the afternoons.
He thought this was just part of getting
older. When we checked his blood
pressure sitting and then standing, it
dropped sharply when he stood up. His
medication dose was simply too strong
for him. After his own doctor adjusted
it, he felt like a different person. His
number went up slightly, his dizziness
disappeared, and his risk of a dangerous
fall dropped.
I share this story because I want you to
understand something very important. A
lower number is not automatically a
better number.
For an older adult, a fall can mean a
broken hip, and a broken hip can change
a person's independence overnight. So
the goal is not the lowest number
possible. The goal is the best number
your body can safely handle.
This is why doctors talk about something
called orthostatic hypotension. That is
a sudden drop in blood pressure when you
stand up. You may feel light-headed,
dizzy, weak, or see spots. It is more
common after 65, especially if you take
certain blood pressure pills, water
pills, or other medicines, or if you are
not drinking enough fluids.
If this happens to you regularly, please
mention it to your doctor, because it is
a very important clue when deciding on
your target.
Now, let's talk about the other side of
the coin because I do not want you to
walk away thinking that a higher number
is fine.
It is not.
Blood pressure that stays high over many
years quietly damages the arteries in
your brain, your heart, your kidneys,
and even your eyes.
It rarely causes any symptoms until the
damage is already done.
That is why it is often called the
silent condition.
You can feel perfectly well and still
have a number that is putting your
future health at risk.
Many studies have shown that in older
adults, lowering a high blood pressure
to a safe level reduces the risk of
stroke, heart failure, and heart
attacks.
It may also help protect memory and
thinking as we age.
So, treating high blood pressure is not
just about numbers on a screen. It is
about protecting your independence, your
mind, and your ability to enjoy your
later years.
So, the real answer is a balance.
Not too high, not too low, and always
personal.
What does personal mean?
Let me describe what your doctor is
quietly thinking about when choosing a
target for you.
First, your overall health.
Someone who is 70, active, walks every
day, and has no major illnesses can
often safely aim for a lower target than
someone who is 85, frail, and has
trouble walking.
Second, your other health conditions.
If you have diabetes, kidney disease, or
have already had a stroke or heart
attack, your doctor may aim for a
tighter target because the benefit of
lower pressure can be greater.
If you have a history of falls,
fainting, or very low readings, your
doctor may be more careful.
Third, your medications. Some
medications interact with blood pressure
pills, and some can cause your pressure
to drop too much, especially when taken
together. Fourth, how well you tolerate
treatment. Some people feel great at
125/75.
Others feel dizzy and weak at the same
reading. Your own body gives important
information that a guideline cannot.
And fifth, your personal goals.
Some people want to stay as active as
possible.
Others are more concerned about avoiding
side effects.
A good doctor will take your priorities
into account.
Now, I want to move to something that
surprises many people. Even the number
itself can be misleading, depending on
how and where it is measured.
Blood pressure changes throughout the
day and even from minute to minute.
It rises when you are nervous, when you
have just climbed the stairs, when you
are in pain, or when you have had a cup
of strong coffee.
It can fall after a meal, during sleep,
or when you are relaxed.
Many people have what is called white
coat hypertension.
Their blood pressure is high in the
doctor's office because they feel
anxious there, but normal at home.
If this is your situation, you could end
up with medication you do not truly
need. On the other hand, some people
have the opposite pattern, called masked
hypertension. Their pressure looks
normal in the clinic, but is high at
home or during daily life. If this is
not noticed, it can quietly cause
damage.
That is why home blood pressure
monitoring can be so valuable for older
adults. But only if it is done
correctly.
Let me walk you through the common
measurement mistakes because they can
change your numbers by 10 or even 20
points.
The first mistake is measuring right
after walking, climbing stairs, or being
active.
Always sit quietly for at least 5
minutes before you measure.
The second mistake is sitting with your
legs crossed or with your feet hanging
in the air.
Sit with your back supported and both
feet flat on the floor.
The third mistake is letting your arm
hang down or resting it on your lap.
Your arm should be supported on a table
with the cuff at about the same level as
your heart.
The fourth mistake is talking, watching
television, or checking your phone while
measuring.
Even a simple conversation can raise the
number.
The fifth mistake is measuring right
after drinking coffee or tea, smoking,
or exercising.
Try to wait at least 30 minutes.
The sixth mistake is using a cuff that
is the wrong size or putting it over a
thick sleeve.
A cuff that is too small can give a
falsely high number. The cuff should be
placed on the bare upper arm.
The seventh mistake is measuring only
once.
Take two readings about 1 minute apart
and note both.
The eighth mistake is using an old or
uncalibrated machine.
Once a year, bring your home monitor to
your doctor's office and compare it with
their device so that you know it is
accurate.
Now, let me share what I consider the
most useful way to track your pressure
at home. For 1 week, measure your blood
pressure twice a day, once in the
morning before breakfast and before your
medication, and once in the evening.
Take two readings each time.
Write them down in a notebook or on your
phone. At the end of the week, bring
that record to your doctor.
That one page of numbers is often far
more valuable than a single reading
taken in a busy clinic. It shows your
true pattern, not just one moment in
time.
Now, let's talk about the most common
mistakes I see around blood pressure in
older adults, and there are quite a few.
Mistake number one is chasing one
perfect number.
Some people become so focused on hitting
exactly 120 over 80 that they become
anxious and check their pressure 10
times a day.
This constant checking can actually
raise the numbers and cause unnecessary
stress.
Checking once or twice a day at the
right times is enough. Mistake number
two is stopping medication because the
number looks good. This is a dangerous
one.
If your blood pressure is normal while
taking your medication, it usually means
the medication is working, not that you
no longer need it.
Never stop or change a blood pressure
medication on your own. If you have side
effects or you feel your numbers are too
low, speak to your doctor who may adjust
the dose.
Mistake number three is ignoring
symptoms of low blood pressure.
Dizziness, light-headedness when
standing, unusual tiredness, blurred
vision, or a feeling that you might
faint are not something to simply live
with. They are worth mentioning to your
doctor. Mistake number four is relying
only on the clinic reading.
As I said, one reading can be
misleading.
Home readings give a much clearer
picture.
Mistake number five is eating too much
salt without realizing it. Most of the
salt in our diet does not come from the
salt shaker. It comes from bread, canned
soups, processed meats, pickles, sauces,
and packaged snacks. Reading labels,
even occasionally, can be eye-opening.
Mistake number six is not drinking
enough fluids,
especially for people who take water
pills.
Dehydration can cause blood pressure to
drop too far and can add to dizziness
and kidney strain.
Mistake number seven is taking
medications at the wrong time or
forgetting doses, then doubling up. Try
to take them at the same time each day
and use a pill box or a simple reminder
to avoid confusion.
Mistake number eight is assuming that a
normal reading means you can skip
regular check-ups. Even when your
numbers are good, kidney function, blood
salts, and your overall risk should be
reviewed regularly.
And mistake number nine is believing
that it is too late to improve. I hear
this often. Doctor, I am 78. Is it still
worth changing anything?
The answer is yes.
Studies show that older adults, even in
their 80s, can benefit from better blood
pressure control and from healthy
lifestyle changes.
It is never too late to protect your
heart and your brain.
So, what can you actually do beyond
medication to support healthy blood
pressure?
This is where small, steady habits make
a real difference.
The first habit is gentle, regular
movement. You do not need a gym.
A daily walk, even 20 or 30 minutes, can
help your arteries stay more flexible
and can lower your blood pressure over
time.
If you cannot walk for 30 minutes at
once, three short walks of 10 minutes
are just as valuable.
The second habit is eating in a way that
supports your heart. Fill more of your
plate with vegetables, fruits, beans,
whole grains, and lean proteins like
fish and chicken. Reduce processed
foods, salty snacks, and sugary drinks.
Foods rich in potassium, such as
bananas, leafy greens, and potatoes can
help balance the effect of salt.
However, if you have kidney problems or
take certain medications, please check
with your doctor first because too much
potassium can be harmful for some
people.
The third habit is reducing salt
gradually.
If you suddenly cut all salt, food may
taste dull and you may give up quickly.
Instead, reduce a little each week and
add flavor with herbs, lemon, garlic,
pepper, and spices.
Your taste buds adjust surprisingly
quickly, often in a few weeks.
The fourth habit is keeping a healthy
weight.
Even a small amount of weight loss can
lower blood pressure in people who are
carrying extra weight.
But for older adults, this should be
done gently and sensibly, without crash
diets, to protect muscle and strength.
The fifth habit is limiting alcohol.
More than a small amount of alcohol
regularly can raise blood pressure and
interfere with some medications.
The sixth habit is protecting your
sleep. Poor sleep and untreated sleep
problems, such as loud snoring with
pauses in breathing, are strongly linked
with high blood pressure. If your
partner has noticed that you stop
breathing at night, or if you wake up
unrefreshed, please mention it to your
doctor.
The seventh habit is managing stress in
a realistic way.
Long-term stress can keep blood pressure
higher than it needs to be. A few
minutes of slow breathing, time
outdoors, a call with a friend, prayer,
music, or a hobby you enjoy are not
luxuries. They are real support for your
heart. And the eighth habit is staying
connected with people. Loneliness has
been linked with poorer heart health. A
regular conversation, a walk with a
neighbor, or a weekly visit with family
may seem small, but it matters more than
people realize.
Now, let me make this practical. Here is
a simple plan you can start this week.
Step one.
Get a validated upper arm home blood
pressure monitor, and ask your
pharmacist or doctor to check that the
cuff size is right for you.
Step two. For 1 week, measure your
pressure twice a day using the correct
method I described. Sit for 5 minutes,
feet flat, back supported, arm at heart
level, no talking.
Step three. Write down every reading.
Add a short note if you felt dizzy,
tired, or unwell that day.
Step four.
Once during the week, check your
pressure sitting, and then again after
standing for 1 to 3 minutes. If the top
number drops by a lot, or if you feel
dizzy, tell your doctor. Step five. Take
your list to your next appointment, and
ask your doctor, "What is the best
target range for me, and why?
That one question can change the whole
conversation.
Step six,
choose two lifestyle habits to start
with. Maybe a daily 10-minute walk, and
swapping one salty snack for a piece of
fruit. Once those feel natural, add
another.
Step seven,
review your medicines with your doctor
or pharmacist at least once a year to
make sure that you are still taking only
what you truly need, and that the dose
is still suit you.
And step eight, keep your numbers in
perspective. A single high or low
reading does not define your health.
Look at the pattern over days and weeks.
I would also encourage you not to change
everything at once. Small, steady steps
are far more effective than dramatic
changes that are hard to maintain.
Let me now answer some questions I often
hear.
People ask me, "Dr. Malik, is 140 over
90 too high after 65?"
In most cases, a reading consistently at
that level deserves attention, and it is
worth discussing with your doctor. But a
single reading does not tell the whole
story. What matters is the pattern,
measured correctly.
Another common question is, "My top
number is high, but my bottom number is
low. Is that normal?"
This pattern is common in older adults
because of stiffer arteries.
It is not unusual, but it is worth
discussing with your doctor because it
influences how treatment is chosen.
People also ask, "Is it dangerous if my
blood pressure is low, like 100 over
60?" If you feel well, and your doctor
knows about it, a lower reading can be
perfectly fine for some people. The
concern arises when low readings come
with dizziness, fainting, weakness, or
falls. The number alone does not tell
you. How you feel matters just as much.
Another question is, "Can I stop my
medication if I feel fine?"
Please do not.
Feeling fine is often exactly because
the medication is working.
If you want to reduce your dose, discuss
it with your doctor first, who can guide
you safely.
People also ask, does my blood pressure
change during the day? Yes. It is
usually lower during sleep, rises in the
early morning, and can vary with
activity, stress, meals, and caffeine.
That is one reason why measuring at
consistent times is so useful.
Another question is, should I check my
blood pressure every day?
For most people who are stable, checking
a few times a week or for a week every
month or two is enough.
If you have just started a new
medication or your doctor asked you to
monitor closely, then daily checks may
be useful. Constant checking though can
create anxiety without giving you better
information. And one more question I
hear often is, do I need to worry about
the bottom number? Both numbers matter,
but after 65, the top number usually
carries more weight in guiding
treatment.
If the bottom number is very low though,
especially with symptoms, it is worth
mentioning to your doctor.
Now, I want to take a moment to speak
about safety and to be very clear about
the limits of what a video can do.
What I have explained today is general
education about how blood pressure
targets are chosen in older adults.
I cannot diagnose your specific
situation, and I cannot tell you what
your personal target should be.
Your own doctor knows your full health
history, your medications, and your
risks, and that is who should guide your
treatment. Please speak to a doctor
promptly if you notice any of the
following: a reading that is very high,
such as 180 over 120 or higher,
especially if you also have a severe
headache, chest pain, shortness of
breath, vision changes, weakness,
confusion, or difficulty speaking.
In that situation, please call your
local emergency number immediately
because this can be a medical emergency.
Also, speak to your doctor if you
experience frequent dizziness when
standing, fainting, or near fainting,
repeated falls, unusual tiredness, a
very slow or very fast heartbeat, or
readings that are consistently much
higher or much lower than your usual
numbers. These do not always mean
something serious, but they deserve
proper evaluation.
And please remember that this video is
for general information and does not
replace medical advice from your own
doctor.
So, let's bring this all together.
The ideal blood pressure after 65 is not
one single magic number. Many guidelines
suggest keeping blood pressure below
roughly 130 over 80 when it can be done
safely, while others accept a slightly
higher range for older adults,
especially if lower numbers cause
problems.
The real answer depends on your overall
health, your medications, your risk of
falls, and how you feel.
What most people never learn is that a
lower number is not always better and
that a high number should never be
dismissed as just part of aging.
The goal is balance.
Protecting your heart, your brain, and
your kidneys without causing dizziness,
falls, or side effects that take away
your independence.
Measure your blood pressure correctly.
Sit quietly, support your back, rest
your arm, and avoid talking.
Keep a simple record for a week. Bring
it to your doctor and ask, "What is my
best target range and why?" Take your
medication as prescribed. Never stop it
on your own. And support your numbers
with small daily habits like walking,
eating more whole foods, reducing salt
gradually, sleeping well, and staying
connected with the people you love.
I would encourage you right now to do
one small thing.
Maybe write down the question you want
to ask your doctor at your next visit.
Or put your blood pressure monitor
somewhere visible. Or decide that
tomorrow morning you will take your
reading the right way.
Sitting quietly for 5 minutes first.
Small, specific actions like these turn
information into protection.
Your blood pressure number is just one
piece of the puzzle.
Understanding what it means and what is
right for you is what truly protects
your health.
Taking small steps like this is exactly
how we protect our health one habit at a
time.
If this video helped you understand your
blood pressure a little better today,
please consider subscribing, share it
with someone you love, and I will see
you in the next one.

What do people who age well actually do every day? Dr. Sami Malik explains five simple golden habits for healthy aging, why each one matters after 60, the common mistakes that undo their benefits, and a realistic plan you can start this week.
In this video, you’ll learn:
 ✅ Why daily movement and strength matter, and what sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) means
 ✅ How much activity health organizations suggest for older adults, in simple terms
 ✅ Simple strength and balance exercises you can start at home, like the chair stand
 ✅ Why protein matters more with age and how to spread it through your day
 ✅ Why thirst weakens with age and how to stay hydrated
 ✅ Simple sleep habits: a steady schedule, morning light, careful naps, and a calm wind-down
 ✅ Why loneliness affects health and how social connection protects your brain and heart
 ✅ Easy ways to keep your mind active and build cognitive reserve
 ✅ Why regular check-ups, vaccines, hearing and vision tests, and yearly medicine reviews matter
 ✅ Common mistakes: doing too much too fast, skipping meals, long naps, isolation, ignoring warning signs
 ✅ A step-by-step plan to start this week, one small habit at a time
 ✅ Warning signs that mean it’s time to talk to your doctor or call emergency services
If you’re over 60 and want to stay strong, independent, and clear-minded, this video will help you build a routine that is simple and realistic.
⚠️ This video is for general educational purposes only and does not replace medical advice from your own doctor. Talk to your doctor before starting a new exercise program, and never stop or change a prescribed medicine on your own. If you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, sudden weakness on one side of the body, sudden confusion, or trouble speaking, call your local emergency number immediately. If you notice unplanned weight loss, persistent low mood, repeated falls, or loud snoring with pauses in breathing, please speak with a healthcare professional promptly.
👉 If you found this helpful, please LIKE, SUBSCRIBE, and turn on notifications so you don’t miss future videos on senior health.
#SeniorHealth #HealthyAging #GoldenHabits #HealthTipsForSeniors #DoctorAdvice #AgingWell

Let me ask you something, and I want you
to answer it honestly, just in your own
mind. When you picture yourself at 80 or
at 85, what do you see? Do you see
someone walking in the garden, cooking a
meal, playing with grandchildren,
traveling, laughing with friends? Or do
you see someone who needs help getting
out of a chair, who rarely leaves the
house, and who is quietly afraid of the
next fall or the next diagnosis?
Most of us want the first picture. And
here is the truth that I have learned
after many years of working with older
adults. The difference between those two
pictures is rarely just luck, and it is
rarely just genes. It is very often made
of small ordinary habits repeated
quietly day after day for years.
Now, you may have noticed the title of
this video says, "Before It's Too Late."
I want to be very clear about what I
mean by that, because I never want to
frighten you. It is never completely too
late to improve your health. I have seen
people in their 80s become stronger,
sleep better, and feel clearer than they
had in years. But it is also true that
the earlier you begin, the more these
habits can protect you, because some
changes in the body are easier to
prevent than to reverse. So, the best
time to start was yesterday. The second
best time is today.
By the end of this video, you will know
five golden habits that doctors see
again and again in people who age well.
You will understand why each one
matters, the common mistakes that undo
its benefits, and a simple realistic
plan to begin this week. I will explain
everything in plain language without
complicated medical words and without
pressure. And I want to ask you for one
small thing as you listen. Do not try to
do all five habits tomorrow. That is how
people get overwhelmed and give up.
Instead, listen for the one or two that
feel most possible for you right now.
That is enough to begin. But first, let
me tell you who I am and why this topic
matters so much to me.
My name is Dr. Sammy Malek. For many
years, I have worked closely with older
adults and I have noticed something that
surprised me early in my career.
The patients who aged most gracefully
were almost never the ones following
some complicated, expensive program.
They were the ones who had a handful of
simple habits that they kept doing
without fuss for decades. A daily walk,
a regular bedtime, a meal that included
real food, a phone call to a friend, a
yearly visit to the doctor, even when
they felt perfectly well.
I have also met people who waited until
a health scare forced them to change.
Many of them recovered more than they
ever expected, but every one of them
told me the same thing afterward. I wish
I had started sooner.
That sentence is the reason I made this
video. I want you to hear it now instead
of later.
Before we continue, if you find this
kind of information helpful, I would
really appreciate it if you considered
subscribing to this channel. Every week,
we break down topics like this one. Real
and practical health information made
simple, especially for people in their
60s, 70s, and beyond.
Subscribing helps more people find these
videos and it helps us keep making them.
Now, let's get into the first golden
habit.
The first golden habit is to move your
body every single day and to include
strength in that movement.
I know, I know. You have probably heard
this advice a thousand times.
But I want to explain it in a way that
you may not have heard before because
understanding why something works makes
it far easier to stick with.
Think of your body as a house that you
plan to live in for another 20 or 30
years.
Your muscles are not just decoration.
They are the frame, the walls, and the
support beams.
They hold you upright, they protect your
joints, they help control your blood
sugar, they support your bones, and they
even send chemical signals that benefit
your brain.
When your muscles are strong, almost
every other system in your body works
better.
But from around the age of 40, we begin
to lose a little muscle every decade.
And after 65, the loss tends to speed up
if we do not give the muscles a reason
to stay.
This age-related loss of muscle has a
medical name, sarcopenia. It is one of
the biggest hidden reasons older adults
lose their independence.
When muscles weaken, walking becomes
slower, balance becomes poorer, falls
become more likely, and a simple fall
can become a broken hip. And a broken
hip, as many families know, can change
everything.
The good news is that muscle responds to
use at almost any age. Research has
shown that older adults, even in their
80s and 90s, can build strength when
they train regularly.
Not by lifting heavy weights in a gym,
but by doing simple, regular movements
that challenge the muscles a little bit
more than usual.
So, what does enough look like?
Health organizations around the world
generally suggest that older adults aim
for about 150 minutes of moderate
activity each week, which is roughly 30
minutes on most days, such as brisk
walking, swimming, cycling, or dancing.
And on at least 2 days a week, they
suggest adding exercises that build
muscle strength and practicing balance.
Let me translate that into real life.
30 minutes does not have to be done all
at once.
Three walks of 10 minutes works just as
well.
Moderate means you can still talk, but
you could not comfortably sing.
Strength exercises can be as simple as
standing up from a chair and sitting
down slowly 10 times, or pressing your
hands against a wall and doing gentle
wall push-ups, or lifting two cans of
beans in each hand.
Balance practice can be as simple as
standing next to a kitchen counter,
holding on lightly, and lifting one foot
for a few seconds.
I once cared for a gentleman in his late
60s who told me, quite proudly, that he
had never exercised a day in his life.
He had worked hard as a shopkeeper,
standing on his feet all day, and he
felt that was enough.
After retiring, he became far less
active, and within 2 years, he noticed
that he was getting breathless on
stairs, and that his legs felt weak when
he stood up from the sofa. He was
frightened, and he told me, "Doctor, I
think it is too late for me."
I told him what I will tell you.
It is not too late. We started very
small. A 5-minute walk each morning, 10
chair stands each evening. Nothing more.
After a month, he increased the walk to
10 minutes.
After 3 months, he was walking 30
minutes a day, and he told me he was
climbing his stairs without stopping. He
said, "I did not know my body still had
this in it."
And that is a feeling I wish for every
person watching this video.
There are a few common mistakes with
this habit.
The first is starting too hard, too
fast.
People who have been inactive often push
themselves, get sore or injured, and
then quit.
Start gently and increase slowly.
The second is doing only walking and no
strength work.
Walking is wonderful for your heart, but
muscle and balance need extra attention.
The third is waiting until you feel
motivated. Motivation usually follows
action, not the other way around. The
fourth is ignoring pain. Mild muscle
soreness is normal, but sharp pain,
chest pain, severe breathlessness, or
dizziness are not, and they deserve a
conversation with your doctor.
If you have a heart condition, severe
arthritis, osteoporosis, or any serious
health problem, please speak with your
doctor before starting a new exercise
routine and ask what kind of movement is
safest for you. In almost every case,
some form of movement is possible and
helpful.
That is the first golden habit. Move
daily and include a little strength and
balance.
The second golden habit is to eat enough
real food with enough protein and to
drink enough fluids.
Now, many people think that healthy
aging means eating less.
And while it is true that older adults
often need slightly fewer calories than
younger people, they do not need less
nutrition. In fact, in some ways they
need more care with nutrition than ever
before. As we age, our bodies become
less efficient at using the protein we
eat to maintain muscle.
That means older adults often need more
protein per meal than younger adults to
get the same benefit. Many experts
suggest that older adults aim for
roughly 1 g of protein per kilogram of
body weight each day or even a little
more, unless a doctor has advised
otherwise because of kidney disease or
another condition. For a person weighing
70 kg, that is about 70 g of protein a
day.
That sounds like a lot, but it is quite
achievable with ordinary food. An egg at
breakfast, a cup of yogurt or a glass of
milk, a serving of fish, chicken, beans
or lentils at lunch and another serving
at dinner along with a handful of nuts
can get most people close. The key point
is to spread protein through the day.
Many older adults eat very little
protein at breakfast and a large amount
at dinner, but muscle seems to benefit
more when protein is distributed across
meals.
Beyond protein, the foundation of
healthy eating in later life is simple.
Plenty of vegetables and fruits, whole
grains, healthy fats such as olive oil,
nuts and fish and less of the things
that cause trouble over time. Heavily
processed foods, sugary drinks and too
much salt. You do not need a perfect
diet.
A steady, mostly wholesome pattern
practiced for years is what protects
your heart, your brain, and your
muscles.
And then there is something that almost
nobody talks about enough.
Water.
As we get older, our sense of thirst
becomes weaker.
This means you can actually be
dehydrated without feeling thirsty. And
dehydration in older adults is not a
small matter. It can cause dizziness,
confusion, constipation, urinary
infections, kidney strain, falls, and
tiredness that people mistake for just
getting old. Many times I have seen an
older patient who seemed confused or
unsteady, and the only thing they needed
was fluids.
So, instead of waiting for thirst, drink
small amounts regularly throughout the
day.
Keep a glass or bottle where you can see
it. Sip when you wake up, with each
meal, with your medication, and in the
afternoon. Tea, soup, milk, and fruits
and vegetables with high water content
all count. Unless your doctor has told
you to limit fluids because of heart or
kidney problems, steady hydration is one
of the simplest protective habits there
is.
Common mistakes with this habit include
skipping meals because you live alone
and do not feel like cooking, relying on
tea and biscuits, eating most of your
protein late in the evening, and
drinking too little water. And if you
are losing weight without trying, please
discuss it with your doctor because
unplanned weight loss can be a sign of
an underlying problem.
That is the second golden habit.
Eat real food, include protein at every
meal, and drink steadily through the
day.
The third golden habit is to protect
your sleep. Sleep is not wasted time. It
is when your body repairs tissue, when
your immune system strengthens, when
your hormones are balanced, and when
your brain sorts and stores memories and
clears away waste products that build up
during the day. Poor sleep over years is
linked with a higher risk of heart
disease, high blood pressure, diabetes,
depression, falls, and memory problems.
Good sleep, on the other hand, protects
almost everything we have talked about
so far. It is normal for sleep to change
with age. It often becomes lighter, and
you may wake more often in the night or
feel sleepy earlier in the evening and
wake earlier in the morning.
But normal change does not mean you must
accept poor sleep. There are simple
habits that make a real difference.
The most powerful one is regularity.
Try to go to bed and wake up at roughly
the same time every day, including
weekends.
Your body has an internal clock, and it
loves consistency.
The second is morning light.
Spending 20 to 30 minutes outdoors in
the morning or sitting by a bright
window helps set your body clock and
supports the natural rise of the sleep
hormone melatonin in the evening. Light
is one of the most underused tools for
better sleep. The third is to be
thoughtful about naps. A short nap of 20
or 30 minutes in the early afternoon can
be refreshing, but a long nap late in
the day can steal sleep from your night.
The fourth is to watch caffeine,
alcohol, and heavy dinners.
Caffeine can stay in an older body for
many hours, so it is wise to avoid
coffee, strong tea, and cola after
midday. Alcohol may make you drowsy, but
it breaks up sleep later in the night.
And a large, rich dinner right before
bed can cause reflux and discomfort. Try
to finish your last meal 2 to 3 hours
before bedtime.
The fifth is a gentle wind down. In the
last hour before bed, dim the lights,
turn off bright screens, and do
something calm.
Reading, soft music, light stretching,
or a warm shower.
Your brain learns to associate this
routine with sleep.
And the sixth is to be careful with
sleeping pills.
Many sleep medicines, including some
over-the-counter products, can cause
confusion, daytime drowsiness, and falls
in older adults.
If you take something for sleep
regularly, please do not stop it
suddenly on your own, but do talk to
your doctor about safer alternatives.
I also want to mention sleep apnea
because it is very common in older
adults and often unrecognized.
Loud snoring, pauses in breathing
noticed by a partner, gasping at night,
waking with a headache, and heavy
daytime sleepiness can all be signs. It
strains the heart and affects memory and
mood, but it can be tested and treated.
Common mistakes with sleep include lying
in bed for hours trying to force sleep,
checking the clock, napping too long,
and relying on sleeping tablets every
night. If you cannot fall asleep after
about 20 minutes, get up, sit in a
comfortable chair in dim light, do
something quiet, and return to bed when
you feel sleepy.
That is the third golden habit. Protect
your sleep and keep a steady rhythm.
The fourth golden habit is to stay
connected with people and to keep your
mind active.
I put these two together because they
work together, and I would like you to
think of this habit as just as important
as exercise or diet because the science
behind it is very strong.
Humans are social beings. When older
adults become isolated or lonely,
research shows that they face higher
risks of depression, poor sleep, heart
problems, a faster decline in thinking
skills, and even earlier death.
That is not meant to scare you. It is
meant to show you how seriously
connection should be taken.
And connection does not require a large
social life.
It can be a daily phone call with a
sibling or friend, a weekly visit with a
grandchild, a regular walk with a
neighbor,
a seat in a community center, a place of
worship, a hobby group, a volunteer
role, or a gentle exercise class.
It is the regularity and the sense of
being known and needed that matters.
Alongside connection, your brain needs
challenge.
Think of your brain as a muscle that
grows stronger when it is used in new
ways. Activities such as reading,
puzzles, card and board games, learning
a few words of a new language, learning
a new recipe, playing an instrument,
gardening, or even learning to use a
smartphone build what scientists call
cognitive reserve. This is a kind of
mental cushion that may help your brain
cope better with the changes that come
with age.
The best activities combine both. A card
game with friends, a choir, a community
garden, a dance class, a group walk with
conversation. These challenge the brain,
the body, and the heart at the same
time.
I remember a gentleman in his early 80s
whose wife had passed away a year
earlier. He had stopped seeing friends,
rarely left the house, and told me,
"There is no point." His appetite had
dropped, his sleep was poor, and he had
become forgetful.
His children were worried about
dementia. A neighbor invited him to a
weekly chess afternoon at the local
community hall.
At first, he went reluctantly. After a
few weeks, he started looking forward to
it.
Within months, his appetite improved,
his sleep improved, and his memory
seemed sharper. His children told me
that he was laughing again. His memory
had not been lost. His life had simply
gone quiet, and it needed to be brought
back to life.
I want to say something very gently to
anyone who feels lonely right now.
Loneliness is not a personal failure.
It is a very common experience,
especially after retirement, after
losing a loved one, or when family lives
far away. If you feel persistently sad,
hopeless, or lose interest in the things
you used to enjoy, please speak with
your doctor. Because low mood is common
in later life, it is treatable, and you
deserve support.
Common mistakes with this habit include
waiting for others to call first,
assuming that you are a burden, turning
down invitations because it feels like
too much effort, and spending most of
the day passively in front of the
television.
That is the fourth golden habit. Stay
connected and keep your mind busy.
The fifth golden habit is to take
prevention seriously, with regular
checkups, and to look after your senses
and your medicines.
This habit is not exciting. It will
never make a dramatic video.
But in my experience, it quietly
protects more people than almost
anything else, because many of the most
serious conditions in later life, such
as high blood pressure, diabetes, high
cholesterol, kidney problems, and
certain cancers, can be silent in their
early stages. You may feel completely
well and still have something that is
quietly causing damage. And early
detection can change the outcome. So,
what should regular checkups include?
Your doctor will advise you based on
your personal history, but in general,
older adults benefit from regular blood
pressure checks, blood sugar and
cholesterol checks, a review of kidney
function, vitamin levels such as vitamin
D and B12 when appropriate, bone health
assessment, and age-appropriate
screening tests. Vaccinations also
matter more with age, including the
yearly flu vaccine and others your
doctor may recommend, because our immune
systems become less strong as we get
older.
Then there are the senses. Vision and
hearing often decline gradually, and
many people adapt without noticing, or
feel embarrassed to mention it. But
untreated hearing loss is strongly
linked with social withdrawal,
loneliness, and faster decline in
thinking skills. Untreated vision
problems increase the risk of falls and
accidents.
A regular eye exam and a hearing test
can open up your world again.
Dental health matters, too, because
chewing problems can limit what you eat.
And finally, medicines.
Many older adults take several
medicines, sometimes prescribed by
different doctors over many years.
It is entirely possible for some to no
longer be needed, or to interact, or to
cause side effects like dizziness,
confusion, or drowsiness.
Once a year, ask your doctor or
pharmacist to review all your medicines,
including supplements and
over-the-counter products.
Bring them all in a bag, or bring a
written list.
This single habit can prevent a
surprising number of problems.
And please remember, never stop or
change a prescribed medicine on your
own.
Common mistakes with this habit include
only seeing a doctor when something is
wrong, skipping screening because of
fear of bad news, hiding hearing or
vision problems, and taking supplements
without telling your doctor.
Finding a problem early is almost always
better than finding it late.
That is the fifth golden habit.
Prevent problems early and check in
regularly.
Now, let me tie these five habits
together because their real power comes
from how they work together.
When you move more, you sleep better.
When you sleep better, your mind is
clearer and your mood is better.
When your mood is better, you are more
likely to socialize and to prepare
nourishing meals.
When you eat well and stay hydrated, you
have more energy to move.
And when you check in with your doctor
regularly, you catch problems early so
that they do not undermine all your
other efforts. Each habit supports the
others, like five threads woven into one
strong rope.
That is why I never encourage people to
fix everything at once.
Choose one habit, practice it until it
feels natural, and let it make room for
the next.
Let me share the most common mistakes I
see when people try to improve their
health in later life.
The first mistake is trying to change
everything at once.
Big overhauls feel inspiring on Monday
and impossible by Friday.
The second mistake is waiting for the
perfect moment.
There is no perfect moment. The best
time to start is today with something
small.
The third mistake is believing that it
is too late.
This belief quietly steals years from
people.
Studies show that older adults, even
those over 80, can improve strength,
balance, mood, and thinking with
consistent effort. The fourth mistake is
chasing quick fixes like miracle
supplements, extreme diets, or expensive
gadgets. Real health is usually built
from boring, consistent habits.
And the fifth mistake is ignoring
warning signs because you do not want to
bother anyone. Your health is worth a
visit to the doctor.
Let me answer a few questions that I
hear often. People ask me, "Dr. Malik,
which of the five habits is the most
important?"
If I had to choose just one place to
start, I would say movement because it
improves sleep, mood, memory, heart
health, and balance all at once.
But the best habit is the one that you
will actually keep doing.
Another question is, "I have arthritis
and my joints hurt. Can I still
exercise?"
In most cases, yes, and movement often
reduces stiffness and pain over time.
Gentle options like water exercise,
cycling, chair-based exercises, and
short slow walks are often well
tolerated. Please check with your doctor
or a physical therapist for what is
safest for you.
People also ask, "Should I take
supplements for healthy aging?" Some
people do need certain supplements, such
as vitamin D or B12, based on blood
tests. But, it is best to decide this
with your doctor, rather than guessing,
because more is not always better, and
some supplements interact with
medicines.
And another common question is, "I live
alone and do not feel like cooking. What
can I do?"
Start with very simple, nourishing foods
that need little preparation. Eggs,
yogurt, canned fish, beans, lentil soup,
fruit, and vegetables you can steam in a
few minutes. You can also cook larger
portions and freeze small ones, or ask a
family member or neighbor to share a
meal.
Now, let me give you a simple plan that
you can start this week.
Step one, choose one habit from today's
video to begin with. Just one. Write it
down.
Step two,
for movement, begin with a 10-minute
walk each day, and add 10 chair stands
in the evening. Increase slowly every
week.
Step three, for nutrition, add one
source of protein to every meal this
week. Keep a glass of water where you
can see it, and sip regularly.
Step four,
for sleep, choose a fixed wake-up time,
and keep it every day. Spend 20 minutes
outside in the morning light.
Step five,
for connection, schedule one regular
call or meeting each week with a friend,
family member, or group. Put it in your
calendar.
Step six,
for your mind, choose one activity you
enjoy, and do it for 15 minutes a day.
Step seven,
for prevention, write down the date of
your last check-up, hearing test, eye
exam, and medicine review, and book
whichever one is overdue.
And remember, do not try to do
everything at once. Small, steady steps
are far more effective than dramatic
changes that are hard to maintain.
Now, I want to take a moment to speak
about safety and to be very clear about
the limits of what a video can do.
What I have explained today is general
education about healthy habits in later
life.
I cannot diagnose your specific
situation and I cannot replace the
advice of your own doctor, who knows
your full health history, your
medicines, and your risks.
Please speak to a doctor before starting
a new exercise program if you have heart
disease, uncontrolled high blood
pressure, severe arthritis,
osteoporosis, or if you have been
inactive for a long time. And please
speak to a doctor promptly if you
experience chest pain or pressure,
severe shortness of breath, fainting,
sudden weakness or numbness on one side
of the body, sudden confusion or trouble
speaking, or a severe headache. In those
situations, please call your local
emergency number immediately.
Also, speak to your doctor if you notice
unplanned weight loss, a big drop in
appetite, persistent low mood or loss of
interest in life, repeated falls, loud
snoring with pauses in breathing, or any
sudden change in memory or behavior.
These do not always mean something
serious, but they deserve proper
evaluation. And please remember that
this video is for general information
and does not replace medical advice from
your own doctor.
So, let's bring this all together.
Healthy aging is not about perfection.
It is not about looking young or never
getting sick or following a strict
program.
It is about giving your body and your
mind the best possible chance to stay
strong, clear, and independent for as
long as possible. And you have five
golden habits to help you do that. Move
your body every day and include a little
strength and balance. Eat real food with
enough protein and drink steadily
through the day. Protect your sleep and
keep a steady rhythm. Stay connected
with people and keep your mind busy and
take prevention seriously with regular
check-ups, careful attention to your
senses, and a yearly review of your
medicines.
Remember what I said at the beginning.
It is not too late. But the sooner you
begin, the more these habits can do for
you. So please, do not wait for a scare
to start.
I would encourage you right now to do
one small thing.
Maybe write down the one habit you want
to start with.
Or put a glass of water where you can
see it.
Or pick up the phone and call someone
you have been meaning to speak to. Or
step outside for a 10-minute walk.
Small specific actions like these turn
information into protection.
Your future self is quietly counting on
the choices you make today. And the
wonderful thing is that those choices
are small, simple, and completely within
your reach.
Taking small steps like this is exactly
how we protect our health, one habit at
a time.
If this video helped you feel a little
more ready to care for your health
today, please consider subscribing,
share it with someone you love, and I
will see you in the next one.

Choking when you’re home alone is one of the most frightening emergencies after 60. Dr. Sami Malik explains what to do in the first 20 seconds, how to help yourself when no one is around, and how to lower your risk of choking in the first place.
In this video, you’ll learn:
 ✅ The difference between partial choking (you can still cough) and complete choking (you can’t breathe or speak)
 ✅ Why the first 20 seconds matter so much when you’re alone
 ✅ How to perform abdominal thrusts on yourself, step by step
 ✅ How to use a sturdy chair or kitchen counter if your hands feel too weak
 ✅ Why you should call your local emergency number right away and keep the line open
 ✅ Common mistakes: waiting too long, drinking water, putting fingers in your throat, running to another room, stopping too early
 ✅ Why choking becomes more likely after 60: weaker swallowing muscles, dry mouth, dentures, and certain medications
 ✅ Simple prevention habits: smaller bites, chewing well, sitting upright, careful pill swallowing
 ✅ Why you should see a doctor after a choking episode, even if you feel fine
 ✅ Warning signs of swallowing problems that mean it’s time to talk to your doctor
If you’re over 60, live alone, or love someone who does, this video will help you feel prepared and know exactly what to do.
⚠️ This video is for general educational purposes only and does not replace first aid training or medical advice from your own doctor. In an emergency, call your local emergency number immediately. If you often cough or choke while eating, feel food getting stuck in your throat, or have a wet or gurgly voice after swallowing, please speak with a healthcare professional promptly.
👉 If you found this helpful, please LIKE, SUBSCRIBE, and turn on notifications so you don’t miss future videos on senior health. Share this video with someone who lives alone.

Imagine this for a moment. You are at
home sitting at your kitchen table. The
house is quiet. Maybe your husband or
wife is out. Maybe your children are at
work. Maybe you simply live alone. And
you are enjoying a quiet lunch. You take
a bite. You swallow. And suddenly
something feels wrong. You try to
breathe in and nothing comes. You try to
cough and nothing comes. You try to call
out and no sound leaves your mouth. Your
heart starts pounding. Your hands fly up
to your throat and in that moment you
realize something that is truly
frightening. There is no one in the room
to help you. This is not a scene from a
movie. This is something that happens in
real homes to real people over the age
of 60 far more often than most of us
like to admit. And the single most
important thing I want you to know today
is this. What you do in the first 20
seconds matters more than almost
anything else. Most people have never
been taught what to do when they are
choking and completely alone. We learn
what to do when someone else is choking.
We have seen the pictures on posters in
restaurants, but almost nobody teaches
us how to save ourselves. And that gap
in knowledge is exactly what I want to
close in this video. By the end of the
next few minutes, you will know exactly
what to do if food or something else
blocks your airway when no one is
around. You will know the very first
thing to do, the exact movement that can
push the blockage out, the mistakes that
waste precious seconds, and the simple
habits that make choking far less likely
to happen in the first place. And I will
explain it all in plain language, step
by step, so that you can remember it
even if panic takes over. I would like
you to do something for me while you
watch. Do not treat this as just another
video. Treat it as a fire drill. The
people who survive emergencies are very
often the people who thought about them
calmly ahead of time. But first, let me
tell you who I am and why this topic
matters so much to me. My name is Dr.
Sammy Malik. For many years, I have
worked closely with older adults,
helping them understand health risks
that are often brushed aside until it is
too late. Over that time, I have spoken
with many families who told me the same
painful sentence afterward. if only we
had known what to do. Choking is one of
those situations. It is fast, it is
frightening, and it is one of the most
preventable causes of sudden emergencies
in older age, especially when a person
has not prepared. What I want you to
understand is that being unprepared is
not your fault. Nobody handed us a
manual. But the good news is that this
is a skill and skills can be learned
even at 60, 70 or 80 years of age. You
do not need to be strong. You do not
need to be young. You simply need to
know what to do and to do it quickly.
Before we continue, if you find this
kind of information helpful, I would
really appreciate it if you considered
subscribing to this channel. Every week,
we break down topics like this one. Real
and practical health information made
simple, especially for people in their
60s,7s, and beyond. Subscribing helps
more people find these videos, and it
helps us keep making them. Now let's get
into what is really happening when
someone chokes. Let's start with the
basics in plain language. Your throat is
actually two pathways that sit very
close together. One pathway carries food
and drink down to your stomach. That is
the food pipe. The other pathway carries
air down to your lungs. That is the
windpipe. At the top, these two pathways
share the same space. And there is a
small flap of tissue like a little door
that closes over the windpipe every time
you swallow. That door is what keeps
food and liquid from going down the
wrong way. Most of the time, this system
works perfectly hundreds of times a day
without you ever thinking about it. But
sometimes a piece of food or a pill or
even a piece of a denture slips toward
the windpipe at the wrong moment or
becomes lodged at the top of it. When
that happens, air cannot reach your
lungs. That is choking. Now there are
two very different situations and
understanding the difference could save
your life. In the first situation, the
blockage is partial. You can still
cough. You can still make some sound,
even if it is a wheezy, squeaky sound.
Air is still moving, even if only a
little. In this situation, your own
cough is the best tool you have. A
forceful cough can move a blockage far
better than almost anything else. So, if
you can cough, keep coughing. Do not
panic. Do not hit yourself on the back
and do not put your fingers down your
throat. Just lean forward slightly and
keep coughing as hard as you can. In the
second situation, the blockage is
complete or nearly complete. You cannot
cough. You cannot speak. You cannot
breathe. You may make no sound at all.
You might notice your face changing
color. This is the emergency we are
talking about today. And this is the
situation where the first 20 seconds
truly matter. Here is why time matters
so much. Your brain depends on a
constant supply of oxygen. When your
airway is completely blocked, that
supply stops. Within a short period,
often less than a minute or two, a
person can become weak, confused, and
may lose consciousness. And once a
person has lost consciousness while
alone, there is nobody to help. That is
exactly why we do not wait. We do not
hope it will pass. We do not walk around
the house looking for water. We act
immediately. So what do we do? Let me
give you the plan and then we will go
through it slowly. First recognize it.
If you cannot cough, cannot speak, and
cannot breathe, you are in a true
choking emergency. Do not wait to see if
it clears. Second, if your phone is
within reach, call your local emergency
number right away and put the phone on
speaker. Even if you cannot speak, leave
the line open if you can. Emergency
operators are trained to respond to
silent calls. And having the call
already connected may help get help
moving while you work on freeing your
airway. Third, and this is the most
important part, begin abdominal thrusts
on yourself immediately. Do not spend
time hunting for your phone if it is not
close. Your first priority is to open
your airway. Let me now describe very
clearly how to do this on your own. Make
a fist with one hand. Place the thumb
side of that fist just above your belly
button and well below the bottom of your
breast bone. Not on your chest, not on
your ribs, but in that soft area of the
upper belly. Now wrap your other hand
around your fist to hold it firmly in
place. Then pull your fist sharply
inward and upward as if you are trying
to lift something up and out. Quick,
firm movements, not a gentle press, a
sharp, strong thrust. And if the first
one does not clear the blockage, repeat
it again and again without stopping
until the object comes out or help
arrives.
The idea behind this movement is simple.
When you press sharply into the upper
abdomen, it pushes the diaphragm upward
which forces a burst of air out of your
lungs like a forceful cough. That burst
of air can push the blockage out.
Now, there is a second method, and it is
especially helpful if you feel too weak
to make strong thrusts with your hands
alone. Find a firm, solid object at
about waist height. A sturdy chair back,
the edge of a kitchen counter, or the
edge of a table will work. Lean forward
and position the upper part of your
belly, that same spot just above your
belly button, against the edge of that
object. Then throw your body weight
forward and downward onto the edge with
a quick hard motion as though you are
trying to fold yourself over it. Let the
edge of the furniture do the pressing
for you. Repeat this motion several
times in a row sharply until the
blockage clears. I want you to picture
this clearly because in a real
emergency, you will not have time to
think. Picture the kitchen counter.
Picture leaning over it. Picture a quick
strong push into your belly. That mental
picture is what you will fall back on.
Now, some of you may be wondering, "Dr.
Malik, what about hitting myself on the
back? What about drinking water? What
about sticking my fingers down my
throat?" These are exactly the questions
I want to answer because the common
instincts in this situation can actually
waste time or make things worse. Let's
talk about the mistakes. The first
mistake is waiting to see if it will
pass. When your airway is fully blocked,
every second counts. Many people
hesitate because they feel embarrassed
or they think maybe it will go away on
its own. If you cannot breathe and
cannot cough, it will not simply go
away. Act right away. The second mistake
is drinking water. It feels natural.
Your throat feels blocked, so you reach
for a glass. But if your airway is
blocked, water has nowhere to go. It can
make the situation worse and waste
precious seconds. Water is for after the
emergency, not during it. The third
mistake is putting your fingers deep
into your throat. If you cannot see the
object clearly, you can push it deeper
and make the blockage worse. Please do
not do this blindly. The fourth mistake
is running outside to find help or
running to another room. When you cannot
breathe, you can lose strength very
quickly. Moving around wastes oxygen and
time. Stay where you are and begin your
thrusts immediately. If you happen to be
close to a neighbor or a family member
and you can reach them in a few steps,
you may signal them, but do not let that
delay the thrusts. The fifth mistake is
panicking and freezing. I understand
this completely. Fear is a natural
reaction, but I want you to remember two
words that can cut through panic. Fist
and thrust. fist above the belly button,
thrust inward and upward. Just repeat
those words to yourself and let your
hands do the work. The sixth mistake is
stopping too early. Sometimes people try
one or two thrusts and when nothing
comes out, they stop. Please keep going.
It may take several thrusts to clear the
blockage. Continue until the object
comes out, until you can breathe again,
or until help arrives. Now, let me
explain why this is such a particular
risk for people over 60. As we get
older, several natural changes happen in
the way we swallow. The muscles in the
throat can weaken slightly. The reflex
that closes the airway when we swallow
can become a little slower. Our mouths
can become drier because we produce less
saliva or because of the medications we
take. And many older adults wear
dentures, which can make it harder to
feel exactly how well food has been
chewed before swallowing.
Certain medications can also make this
worse. Some medications cause dry mouth,
others cause drowsiness. Alcohol and
sedating medications can dull the
reflexes that protect the airway. And
some health conditions such as a
previous stroke, Parkinson's disease, or
other nerve and muscle conditions can
affect swallowing even further. And none
of this means that every older adult is
in danger every time they eat. But it
does mean the margin for error becomes a
little smaller as we age. And that is
why a little preparation goes a long
way. Let me tell you about a
conversation I once had with a patient,
a retired gentleman in his late7s who
lived alone. He told me that a few
months earlier he had been eating a
piece of meat at his table when it
suddenly lodged in his throat. He could
not cough. He could not speak. He told
me his first thought was to get a glass
of water and he stood up and began
walking toward the kitchen. Halfway
there, he realized the water would not
help and something he had once read came
back to him. He leaned over the back of
a kitchen chair and pushed hard into his
stomach again and again. After several
attempts, the piece of meat came out. He
told me that his hands were shaking for
the rest of the day, but he was alive.
and he said something I have never
forgotten. He said, "The only reason I
knew what to do is because I had thought
about it once long before. I share this
story not to frighten you, but to remind
you that knowledge, even if you only
half remember it, can make the
difference between panic and action."
Now, let's talk about prevention.
Because the best way to survive choking
is to make sure it never happens in the
first place. The most important habit is
to slow down.
Many choking episodes happen when
someone is rushing, distracted, or
eating while talking, laughing, or
watching television. Try to give your
meal your full attention, at least for
the first few minutes. Sit upright at
the table, not on the sofa or in bed,
and not leaning back. Take smaller bites
than you think you need. Chew each bite
thoroughly before swallowing. If the
food is something dense, like meat or
bread, chew a little longer. Take a sip
of water between bites if your mouth
feels dry, but make sure you have
swallowed the food completely first. Be
careful with foods that carry a higher
risk. Large pieces of meat, especially
if they are tough, soft white bread that
can form a sticky ball, sticky foods
like peanut butter eaten by the
spoonful, whole grapes, hard candy,
nuts, and dry crumbly foods. These are
not forbidden, but they deserve extra
attention. Cut them smaller, soften
them, or pair them with something moist.
If you wear dentures, make sure they fit
properly. Loose dentures can make
chewing harder and can even become a
hazard themselves. If you have noticed
that they feel loose, see your dentist
because a small adjustment can make a
big difference. Be careful with pills.
Many older adults take several tablets a
day, and larger pills can sometimes get
stuck on the way down. Swallow them with
a full glass of water sitting upright
one at a time. If you have trouble
swallowing certain pills, do not crush
them or cut them on your own. Ask your
doctor or pharmacist whether another
form is available. Avoid eating when you
are very tired, drowsy, or after
drinking alcohol. These states can slow
down the protective reflexes that keep
your airway safe. And pay attention to
the warning signs. If you notice that
you often cough or choke when eating or
drinking. If food seems to stick in your
throat, if you have a wet or gurgly
voice after swallowing, or if you find
yourself avoiding certain foods because
they are hard to swallow, please talk to
your doctor. These are signs of what is
called a swallowing difficulty, and it
can often be evaluated and managed. A
swallowing specialist can sometimes
teach you simple techniques and posture
changes that make eating much safer.
Now, let me help you make this practical
because information is only useful if
you can actually use it in the moment.
Here is a simple way to prepare starting
today. Step one, keep your phone within
reach whenever you eat, especially if
you live alone. It can be on the table
beside you. This small habit means that
if something does go wrong, you are not
wasting time looking for it. Step two,
know your local emergency number by
heart and make sure it is saved clearly
on your phone. In a moment of panic,
even simple things can slip from memory.
Step three, practice the movement
gently. Stand in your kitchen, make a
fist, and place it just above your belly
button below your breast bone. Wrap your
other hand around it. Practice the
inward and upward motion slowly without
any force. The goal is simply to teach
your hands where to go. Then practice
leaning over the back of a chair so that
you know exactly how it feels.
Practicing without force is important
because real thrusts are strong and you
should never use that force unless you
are truly choking. Step four, tell
someone close to you what you have
learned. Let a neighbor, a friend, or a
family member know that you live alone
and that you have been learning about
choking emergencies. Ask them to check
in with you regularly. A simple daily
phone call can be a safety net in many
situations.
Step five, consider taking a basic first
aid course. Many local community
centers, hospitals, and health
organizations offer short courses, and
they teach you to respond to choking,
not only in yourself, but in others.
This is one of the most valuable few
hours you can spend. Step six, make your
eating space safe. Sit at a table with a
sturdy chair. Keep the area around it
clear so that if you need to lean over a
surface, you can do it quickly. Do not
eat while standing, walking around, or
lying down. Step seven, take a moment
before your next meal to remind yourself
of the three words: fist, thrust,
repeat. Say them quietly and let them
become part of your mind. This kind of
mental rehearsal makes the response far
more automatic when it counts. I would
also encourage you not to try to change
everything at once. Pick two or three of
these steps to begin this week and add
more as they become part of your
routine. Let me now answer a few
questions I often hear. People ask me,
"Dr. Malik, is it really possible to do
this on my own? I am not strong." The
answer is that it does not require great
strength. It requires correct position
and quick, firm movements. Using the
edge of a chair or counter allows your
body weight to do much of the work. And
that is why I teach this method to
people who feel they are not strong.
Another common question is, "What if I
have a health condition like a bad back,
a hernia, or a recent surgery? Can I
still do abdominal thrusts?" In a true
life-threatening choking emergency,
opening the airway is the priority. And
most doctors would agree that saving
your life comes first. But this is
exactly the kind of question I encourage
you to discuss with your own doctor
ahead of time so that you know what is
safest for your particular situation.
People also ask what if I am pregnant or
very overweight so that I cannot reach
properly. Those situations may need a
slightly different technique and that is
a very good reason to take a first aid
course where trainers can show you the
alternatives in person. Another question
is I managed to clear the blockage. Am I
fine now? This is very important. Even
if the object comes out and you feel
completely well, you should still see a
doctor soon afterward. Abdominal thrusts
are forceful and they can sometimes
cause bruising or injury to organs in
the upper belly. Also, part of the
object may remain or the airway may be
irritated or swollen. A doctor can check
you over properly. If you feel any pain,
difficulty breathing, a persistent
cough, or trouble swallowing afterward,
please seek medical care right away.
People also ask, "Why do I sometimes
cough when I drink, even when nothing
gets stuck?" That can be a sign that
liquids are sometimes slipping toward
the airway, and it is worth mentioning
to your doctor, particularly if it
happens regularly. And another important
question, what if I am eating with
someone and they are choking? This video
is mainly about helping yourself, but
the same principles apply. If someone
beside you is choking and cannot cough
or speak, call for emergency help and
begin the standard rescue with firm back
blows followed by abdominal thrusts. And
if they become unresponsive, you will
need to begin chest compressions and
follow the instructions from emergency
services. Again, a hands-on course is
the best way to learn this properly. Now
I want to take a moment to speak about
safety and to be very clear about the
limits of what a video can do. What I
have explained today are widely
recommended general first aid principles
for a choking emergency. But I cannot
diagnose your specific situation and I
cannot replace training in person or the
advice of your own doctor who knows your
complete health history. You should
speak with your doctor if you notice any
of the following. Frequent coughing or
choking during meals. A feeling that
food gets stuck in your throat or chest,
unexplained weight loss, repeated chest
infections or pneumonia, a horse or wet
sounding voice after eating, or if you
find that you are avoiding foods because
swallowing has become uncomfortable.
These are all signs that your swallowing
deserves a proper evaluation.
And in any emergency where you cannot
breathe, always remember that emergency
services exist for exactly this reason.
Do not hesitate to call them and do not
feel embarrassed. It is always better to
call and not need help than to need help
and not call. So, let's bring this
together. Choking when you are alone is
one of the scariest situations an older
adult can face. But it is also one of
the situations where knowing what to do
can truly make a difference. Remember
that if you can still cough, you keep
coughing. If you cannot cough, cannot
speak, and cannot breathe, you act
immediately. You do not wait. You do not
reach for water. You call for help if
your phone is within reach. And you
begin abdominal thrusts right away using
your fist above your belly button or by
leaning over the edge of a sturdy chair
or counter. You keep going until the
blockage clears or help arrives. And
afterward you see a doctor, even if you
feel fine. Most importantly, remember
that prevention is your strongest
protection. Slow down when you eat. Take
small bites. Chew well. Sit upright.
Keep your phone close. And pay attention
to the early signs that your swallowing
may be changing. I would encourage you
right now to take just a moment to do
